title: Why was Java 8 introduced over Java 7, and what are its major features?
keyPoints: Java 8 (2014) was the biggest release in Java history, adding functional programming to a purely object-oriented language.
Lambda expressions let you pass behaviour as data, replacing verbose anonymous inner classes with concise one-liners.
The Stream API provides declarative data-processing pipelines: filter, map, reduce, and collect replace manual for-loops.
Optional wraps a possibly-absent value, forcing explicit null handling and eliminating accidental NullPointerException.
Default methods on interfaces enable backward-compatible API evolution without breaking existing implementations.
The java.time API replaced the broken, mutable Date and Calendar with immutable, thread-safe LocalDate, Instant, and ZonedDateTime.
Method references like Trade::getAmount and CompletableFuture for async composition round out the feature set.

s1_definition.oneliner: Java 8 added lambdas, streams, Optional, java.time, and default methods, transforming Java from a purely imperative language into a hybrid OOP plus functional language.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Lambda expressions** let you write concise anonymous functions and pass behaviour as data instead of creating anonymous inner classes.
- **Functional interfaces** such as `Predicate`, `Function`, `Consumer`, and `Supplier` provide the single-abstract-method types that lambdas target.
- **Stream API** offers declarative pipelines: `filter`, `map`, `reduce`, and `collect` replace explicit for-loops with composable operations.
- **Optional** is a null-safe container that makes absent values explicit in the type system.
- **Default methods** on interfaces allow adding new methods like `Collection.stream()` without breaking millions of existing implementations.
- **java.time API** provides immutable, thread-safe date and time classes that replace the broken `Date`, `Calendar`, and `SimpleDateFormat`.
s1_definition.analogy: Before Java 8, Rajesh at National Bank of India needed 50 lines of for-loops, temporary lists, and manual threading to process 100,000 account transactions. After Java 8, the same report is one readable pipeline: `transactions.stream().filter(Transaction::isSettled).map(Transaction::getAmount).reduce(BigDecimal.ZERO, BigDecimal::add)`. It is like upgrading from hand-written ledgers to an automated reconciliation system that can parallelise with a single method call.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Java 7 (Imperative)              Java 8 (Hybrid OOP + Functional)
  ────────────────────              ──────────────────────────────────
  Anonymous inner class     ──→     Lambda expression
  Manual for-loop           ──→     Stream pipeline
  null return               ──→     Optional<T>
  Date / Calendar           ──→     java.time (LocalDate, Instant)
  Interface = abstract only ──→     default + static methods
  Future.get() blocks       ──→     CompletableFuture chains
  Manual thread pool        ──→     parallelStream()
```

```text
  Stream Pipeline (source → intermediate → terminal)
  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  transactions.stream()          ← SOURCE
       │
       ▼
  .filter(Transaction::settled)  ← INTERMEDIATE (lazy)
       │
       ▼
  .map(Transaction::amount)      ← INTERMEDIATE (lazy)
       │
       ▼
  .reduce(ZERO, BigDecimal::add) ← TERMINAL (triggers all)
       │
       ▼
  Rs.373000.50                   ← RESULT
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Java 8 was the most significant release in Java history, transforming the language from purely imperative to a hybrid object-oriented and functional style. Lambda expressions pass behaviour as data, eliminating verbose anonymous inner classes. The Stream API provides declarative data-processing pipelines where filter, map, reduce, and collect replace manual for-loops with readable, composable operations. Optional eliminates NullPointerException by forcing explicit handling of absent values. The java.time API replaced the broken, mutable Date and Calendar with immutable, thread-safe classes.

In Rajesh's settlement report service at National Bank of India, the Java 7 version required 50 lines of imperative code with manual counters, null checks, and anonymous Comparator classes. The Java 8 version produces the identical report in 15 lines of declarative stream pipelines. The stream approach is also easier to parallelise: replacing `stream()` with `parallelStream()` distributes the work across multiple cores with zero code changes.

Default methods on interfaces enabled backward-compatible API evolution. The Java team added `forEach()`, `stream()`, and `removeIf()` to existing interfaces without breaking a single implementing class. Method references like `Transaction::amount` and `BigDecimal::add` make code read like English. CompletableFuture replaced blocking `Future.get()` with non-blocking composition. Together, these features form the standard way to write Java in every modern banking application.

Remember one sentence: Java 8 added lambdas, streams, Optional, java.time, and default methods, turning Java from purely imperative into a hybrid functional language.
